I don't necessarily agree that intelligence can solely be determined by genetics. Althought genetics do play a role on how a person absorbs information. Depending on how predisposed that person is to learn and care wether something is true or not, determines their "intelligence" or rather their knowledge. I personally love to learn new things about specific subjects and to question my beliefs, to make sure they're genuine and up-to-par with the evidence. Those subjects range from religion, biology, cosmology, and philosophy. Thanks to my thirst for knowledge I came from being a Christian, gay-hating person, to being an atheist, respectful, and having a relatively tolerant point of view.

I don't know of any studies on the subject of there were it would have to be a twin study to have much validity. Perhaps siblings would be a fairly decent study as well.

The best, and most widely accepted theory, is that both are important but genetics ultimately dictates the extent of out potential. How hard we work determines how much of that potential is filled, among other nuture type factors.

So for example a child born to two genius parents should have very high potential, but if they spend thier life doing heroin and never working their brain is going to mush. So I'm sorry ,but your answer is it depends on a lot of factors.

Lots of text and no numbers in here. Hunt (2011) concluded that in post-industrial societies 40-60% of the variation in intelligence scores was due to genetic variation.
